title: Officially corrected errors persist in AI training data
content:
Officially corrected errors persist in AI training data: Céphéide public alert, data and proofs
Description
Public alert by Céphéide, Loxyn's measurement bench, with all data, scripts, readings and proofs. French and English texts of the alert are in ALERTE/; the step-by-step guide is 00 — LISEZ-MOI.md. The full package (every step folder, lists, proofs) is in the zip file; MANIFESTE.sha256 gives the SHA-256 of each file it contains.
Official texts are corrected after publication: EU corrigenda in the Official Journal, verified RFC errata, retractions of scientific papers. We measured whether these corrections are present in public datasets used to train language models (EurlexResources, FineWeb-2, a FineWeb sample, peS2o) and what models answer about the corrected passages. Main results: 95.5% of testable single-language corrections to EU acts (1,989/2,082) remain in their erroneous form in EurlexResources; at least 124 corrected EU-law errors and 60 verified RFC errata are reproduced in web training data; about 12,200 retracted papers are in peS2o, 79% with no mention of the retraction; 53% of a random sample of retracted papers are still cited a year or more after retraction (OpenAlex); asked without documents, five models give the erroneous version in 45% of the answers in which they commit to one version, and one answer in 295 says it does not know. Shown both versions side by side, the models choose the corrected one in 53% of cases, and naming the act makes no difference; when each version carries its date and the corrigendum label, the four larger models choose it in 99–100% of cases.
Every step was preregistered and its fingerprints timestamped with OpenTimestamps in the Bitcoin blockchain. Failed controls, lost bets and deviations are reported. The Retraction Watch file is not redistributed (its SHA-256 is in the seal of the retraction step).

report.summary: A preregistered audit finds corrected EU-law errors, RFC errata and retracted papers still sit in major LLM training corpora, and models often repeat the stale version.
report.background: Official corrections are routine: corrigenda in the EU Official Journal, verified IETF RFC errata, and journal retractions. But web-scale training corpora are assembled as frozen snapshots — bulk downloads and crawls captured once and rarely re-validated. Nothing in a typical pipeline propagates a later correction back into text that was already scraped, and derived documents (quotes, mirrors, summaries) keep circulating the original wording. Datasets such as EurlexResources, FineWeb-2 and peS2o are widely used and well documented on scale and filtering, but their correctness over time is essentially unmeasured. Because language models learn from statistical co-occurrence, an error repeated consistently across millions of documents looks indistinguishable from a fact. Loxyn's Céphéide measurement bench preregistered every step and timestamped file fingerprints with OpenTimestamps on Bitcoin, making the audit tamper-evident and publishing failed controls and deviations alongside the results.
key_points: Corrections never reach the legal corpus: 95.5% of testable single-language corrections to EU acts (1,989 of 2,082) are still present in their erroneous form in EurlexResources. The dataset is a snapshot of legal text, so a corrigendum published later simply has no path into it.

Errors propagate into general web data: at least 124 corrected EU-law errors and 60 verified RFC errata were reproduced inside web-derived training data, including FineWeb-2 and a FineWeb sample. Because web pages quote and mirror official sources, one stale document becomes many.

Retractions are effectively invisible: roughly 12,200 retracted papers appear in peS2o, 79% with no mention of the retraction, and 53% of a random sample of retracted papers were still being cited a year or more after retraction according to OpenAlex.

Asked cold, models repeat the error: given no documents, five models returned the erroneous version in 45% of answers where they committed to one version, and only 1 answer in 295 admitted not knowing. The failure is silent rather than hedged.

Models can be steered, but only with help: shown both versions side by side they picked the corrected one just 53% of the time — naming the act made no difference — yet when each version carried its date and a corrigendum label, the four larger models chose correctly in 99-100% of cases.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this reframes data quality: filtering, deduplication and toxicity work are mature, but temporal correctness and provenance are not. Corpora need versioning, correction links and auditable lineage, and vendors selling legal, medical or standards-adjacent systems inherit a silent liability. For developers, the lesson is that parametric knowledge cannot be trusted for versioned documents — retrieval from authoritative, corrigenda-aware sources, citation checking, and explicit date/label metadata in prompts are the practical mitigations, and the study shows labelling works. For regular users, the risk is confident, plausible, outdated answers about regulations, technical standards and scientific findings, delivered without any signal that a correction exists. Expect provenance standards, dataset freshness benchmarks and correction-aware retrieval to become procurement requirements.
report.tools: Follow the audit trail via the Zenodo record and Céphéide package (MANIFESTE.sha256, OpenTimestamps proofs). To reproduce or extend it: EurlexResources, FineWeb-2 and peS2o as test corpora; the Retraction Watch database (not redistributed here) and OpenAlex for retraction and citation status; IETF errata for RFC checks; datatrove for rebuilding pipelines; WIMBD for auditing what is actually inside a corpus; and Croissant metadata plus Data Provenance Initiative cards for documenting lineage and freshness.
